raw_case_text:
This is a 21-year-old Moroccan patient residing in a rural area in the vicinity of Laarach (North of Morocco), with regular contact with his own dog for a year. The history of the disease dates back to 2010 marked by the onset of mild pain in the right hypochondrium.
In 2022, the patient was admitted in our hospital in the Vascular Surgery Department for sought medical attention due to an increase in the pain in the right hypochondrium accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Abdominal radiography [ultrasound (US) and computed tomography (CT)] revealed multiple hydatid cysts in the liver (four cysts in segments VII and VI, three of which were unilocular and one multilocular, measuring 105x90 mm, 83x31 mm, 43x28 mm and 30x19 mm) and peritoneum (the cysts were unilocular, five in the left iliac fossa, measuring approximately 30x24 mm, and one in the right iliac flank, measuring 25x38 mm). The cysts were classified as type IV according to the Gharbi classification, and type CE1, CE2 and CE3a according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification.
Hydatid serology performed in a private laboratory in Laarach, using the indirect haemagglutination technique (IHA), was positive [the titre >1280 (the positivity threshold is >=320)].
Medical treatment with albendazole (800 mg/day) was initiated and the patient was regularly monitored in consultation every 3 months in our hospital.
After 9 months of daily medical treatment, a follow-up CT scan revealed a large hepatic hydatid cyst in the right lobe, spanning segments V, VI, VII and VIII, measuring 123x108x123 mm. Peritoneal dissemination was observed in the inter-hepato-phrenic space and along the Arantius groove (Fig. 1).
Clinically, the patient was stable with constant pain in the right hypochondrium, respiratory function was without abnormalities, and the chest x-ray performed at a private radiology centre was normal.
Laboratory parameters, liver function tests [aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT)] and complete blood count showed no abnormalities (the eosinophil level was normal). Hydatid serology performed in our laboratory indicated a titre of 30.30 NTU [Novalisa Echinoccus IgG, ELISA (the positivity threshold is 11 NTU)].
Surgical treatment was proposed and a median laparotomy straddling the umbilicus was performed. Intra-operatively, multiple cysts of varying sizes were discovered, involving almost the entire right hepatic lobe, along with the gall bladder intact, the greater omentum, the mesentery, the small intestine, the pelvis, subhepatic and pre- and latero-rectal areas.
All of the extracted surgical specimens were sent to the parasitology laboratory for examination. The macroscopic examination of the samples revealed several pieces of different sizes from various locations (Fig. 2).
Upon microscopic examination of the contents obtained by scraping the internal face of each cuticle, hooks of E. granulosus were identified at the pelvic part. Additionally, hooks, invaginated and devaginated scolex of this parasite were observed in the peritoneal and hepatic parts. The 0.2% eosin viability test indicated non-viable scolex of E. granulosus (Figs3  4).
All the epidemiological (endemic region, exposure with dog), clinical, radiological and parasitological data confirmed the diagnosis of disseminated hydatid disease.
After the operation treatment, medical treatment with albendazole (800 mg/day) was continued, and the patient was regularly monitored (biologically and clinically) every 3 months in our hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old Moroccan patient presented with worsening right hypochondriac pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting on a 12-year background of mild right upper quadrant pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient's illness began in 2010 with mild right hypochondriac pain. In 2022, the pain intensified and was accompanied by nausea and vomiting, prompting hospital admission. Despite 9 months of oral albendazole (800 mg/day), constant right hypochondriac pain persisted and follow-up imaging demonstrated cyst enlargement and peritoneal dissemination.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resided in a rural area near Laarach (Northern Morocco) and had regular contact with a pet dog for 1 year.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic/worsening right hypochondriac pain, nausea, and vomiting; negative for respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Clinically stable with constant right hypochondriac tenderness/pain and normal respiratory examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count (including eosinophil count) and liver function tests (AST, ALT) were normal. Chest X-ray was normal. Initial private-lab Echinococcus IHA serology was positive (titer >1280; threshold >=320), and hospital Novalisa Echinococcus IgG ELISA was positive at 30.30 NTU (threshold 11 NTU). Abdominal ultrasound showed multiple hepatic and peritoneal hydatid cysts.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial abdominal CT revealed four hepatic cysts in segments VI and VII (105 x 90 mm, 83 x 31 mm, 43 x 28 mm, and 30 x 19 mm; Gharbi type IV / WHO CE1, CE2, CE3a) and six unilocular peritoneal cysts (five in the left iliac fossa ~30 x 24 mm and one in the right iliac flank 25 x 38 mm). Repeat CT after 9 months of albendazole showed progression to a 123 x 108 x 123 mm right hepatic lobe cyst (segments V-VIII) with peritoneal dissemination in the inter-hepato-phrenic space and Arantius groove. Median laparotomy excised multiple cysts from the right hepatic lobe, greater omentum, mesentery, small intestine, pelvis, and subhepatic/perirectal spaces; parasitological microscopy of cuticle scrapings identified E. granulosus hooklets and invaginated/devaginated protoscolices (non-viable on 0.2% eosin staining).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated hepatic and peritoneal cystic echinococcosis (Echinococcus granulosus), confirmed by positive IHA (>1280) and IgG ELISA (30.30 NTU) serologies and parasitological identification of hooklets and non-viable protoscolices. Following 9 months of preoperative albendazole (800 mg/day) and median laparotomy with multi-site cyst excision, postoperative albendazole (800 mg/day) was continued with quarterly clinical and biological follow-up.
